Uniform Title: Mokṣasopāna Main Title: Mokṣasopāna with Commentary (Tīkā) Author: Kāṇḍadvayātītayogī
Manuscript: NGMCP manuscript No. 1-1397, Reel No. A-179/8. Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski:
Nothing is known about the author of the *Mokṣasopāna* or the author of...

The *Tīkā*. According to the *Catalogus Catalogorum*, he was called Kāṇḍadvayātītayogī. The goddess Kubjikā is mentioned a dozen times, and a number of verses from the root text can be traced [to her].
The Kubjikā Tantras. This work treats the stages of yoga and internal worship in the characteristic style of the Kubjikā Tantras.
Notes: Revision 0: November 15, 2014.

Country of publication: India. Oṃ namaḥ śivaśaktaye.
I bow to Śiva-Śakti, who transcends the void, who is supreme and tranquil,
who is the power of Śambhu through Śiva, and who is utterly free from both existence and non-existence.
"Oṃ, homage be to you, O Mahāmāyā!"—thus the meaning of the sūtra should be stated. This is the first [explanation] of the syllable *oṃ*.

Through the distinction of the sounds of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, it is called *oṃ*. *A* is Brahmā, *u* is Viṣṇu, and *m* is Maheśvara; therefore, it is called *oṃ*. By virtue of pervading the three worlds, within the reality (*satva*) of *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*, [it encompasses] the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, as well as the worlds of gods, demons, and humans, and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M—these are the letters A and M; and the letter M is indeed the bindu.
Through the union of the letters *a* and *u*, the letter *m* is said to be at the end; through the union with the *bindu*, the letter *m* is called the great seed-syllable of Śiva.
Therefore, it is proclaimed that the mantra is preceded by the syllable *oṃ*. Another says:
The Half-moon, the Obstructing One, Sound, and the End of Sound;
likewise Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.
The net of bonds extends up to the level of *samanā*, while the supreme *Śiva* extends up to *unmanā*;
by that, the entire universe is manifested, as is the supreme origination itself.
Regarding the term "half-moon":

The *amṛtabindu* (drop of nectar) is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) by virtue of its nature as Śiva and its form as the sustainer of the universe. Therefore, the state of perfection (*niṣpatti*) occurs within this very [half-moon] which possesses sixteen digits (*kalā*). How are there sixteen digits? They consist of the lunar days beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
The seed, the great fire, water, wind, the destroyer of the earth,
the wielder of power, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self are like moths [flying into the flame].
The mountain-joy (Girīnanda), the five directions, and the pure one (Śuddhaka) are all-pervading;
therefore, it is called the "half-moon" (ardhacandra), established above Śiva.
He said: "Cessation."

1b) *Nigatarodhī* refers to that wherein cessation (*nirodha*) occurs. It is the state of pervading space and the elements. *Nirodhī* is bondage. Regarding the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, it is said: "It is not [merely] sound. Sound (*nāda*) is a specific resonance (*dhvani*). It is both unmanifest (*avyakta*) and manifest (*vyakta*); here, it is the unmanifest.

Śiva is the Manifest (Vyakta); Śakti is Speech (Vāṇī), whose essential nature is Sound (Nāda). Sound is all-pervasive, extending from the subterranean realms (Pātāla) up to Śiva, and is the form of the universe. Sound consists of three aspects: Pure (Śuddha), Salangaka (Sālaṅga), and Mixed (Saṃkīrṇa). In the Pure [state], it is the movement; the Salangaka is Śakti. The state of the two being in a state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva) is called Mixed.
The pure sounds are fivefold: namely, the sound of a lamp-flame, the sound of a conch, the sound of a lute, the sound of a drum, and the sound of a bell.
They say Gāndhāra is the fifth mantra; it is prescribed as the pure sound (śuddhanāda).
These are the secondary characteristics (parāṅgas). When combined with the pure sāraṅga, it is called *sakīrṇa*; therefore, it is not termed *nāda*.
They say that its true nature consists of six kinds of sounds.
2a) For example:
Just as a lamp and so forth [illuminate] when all colors are manifested,
therefore Mādhava is celebrated by the name Dīpaka (the Illuminator).
I am not one who has not reached the end of sound.

"Ending with *nāda*": this refers to the specific mantras beginning with *gāyatrī* and extending up to the dissolution (*laya*) of the mantra. This is because at the end of *nāda*, the function of all mantras is accomplished. [The syllables] *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *phaṭ*, *ṭha*, and so forth, are to be employed at the ends of the *nādas*. "By means of power" (*śaktyā*).
Will, action, knowledge, the substratum, and so forth are [the powers] because of their pervasiveness. Thus ends the section on Power (śakti).

"Having been able [to do so], she is Śakti. And likewise in the Uttara-tantra: "The light-filled, victory-bestowing, world-nourishing Śakti, who awakens beings from the pot (kumbha) up to those at the end of the age of Yoga; the mistress who ferries one across the ocean of existence and the suffering of birth and so forth; the Mistress of the Left (Vāmeśī), who establishes the path of the Vāma-kula, she is triumphant."
For it is thus:

I perpetually bow to the digit of the moon within the six paths; she who dwells there, stainless, eternal in form, partless, a portion of Śakti, residing in the body of Śiva, and present for the sake of the glorious vision. She resides in the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) within the limbs of Saṃvara, white with excellent qualities, partless in the form of light, in the lotus of omniscient knowledge.

In the center of the one who grants boons and fearlessness, the awakened consciousness, resides Śī, the supreme Paramaśivā, who is stainless, possesses infinite power, is the mistress of accomplishments, the bestower of supreme bliss, and has conquered all remaining powers; to her I offer salutation.

Such is the power (*śakti*). Regarding the term "pervasive" (*vyāpinīm*): she is pervasive even in the center, extending up to the end of Śiva. At the end of Śiva is the one called Śivā; she is the soul of all, the omnipresent Lord, the creator and destroyer of the universe, who revolves at the end of Śiva.
She is the pervasive one. "Samanā" means the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti) in a state of aesthetic fusion (samarasībhāva).
3a) It is taught that there are two kinds of mental activity (*manas*): the pure and the impure.
Impure is the operation of desire; pure is that which is devoid of desire.
I am uplifted by the teaching.

Freed from existence and non-existence, the Transmental (*unmanā*) is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) by virtue of its pervasiveness over the gross and the subtle; it is the Transmental. Being of the nature of the bliss of awakening, it is the state (*bhāva*); the mind is the power of darkness (*tāmasī*). That which is liberated from time and power is called the Transmental, the *Kula*. That Transmental is the "end of the Samanā" (*samanānta*), meaning that at which the end of the Samanā occurs.
Beheld by Śiva, he is equal to a god in his own office.

The Sage (Ṛṣi) is said to extend up to the level of Samanā, having become transcendent and pervading the void; he is thus "together with the limit of Samanā. "The net of bonds" (pāśajāla) refers to the net of bonds belonging to the fetters (pāśa).
The noose is twofold, consisting of demerit and merit; by means of the noose of merit and the noose of demerit, living beings remain on the side of Śivā.
Having seen it, that which was unseen is not obtained; then the "net of snares" (pāśajāla) is spoken of. That is the net of snares. It ends with the Transmental (unmanānta).
Beyond the Unmanā state is the end of Unmanā. [He] spoke thus regarding the end of Unmanā: "Bliss, supreme bliss, and innate bliss; the fourth, the beyond-the-fourth, and the end of Unmanā."
Thinking thus: "The other" means the nature of the other. From that supreme [state], one becomes the essential nature of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth.

At the end of transmigratory existence, the supreme station is declared through pure knowledge; it is the bound soul (paśu) joined with fetters, yet purified, possessing the state of a pure self, situated within both the Akula and Kula, and merged with Brahmā, the gods, and so forth.
Victorious is the Lord, the Sovereign of the Mistress of the Left, whose nature is eternal and partless; he is the supreme essential form.

Regarding the term *Śiva*: He is eternally peaceful, partless, light, and endowed with all powers and so forth; being undivided and pervading the universe, he is called *Paraśiva*. And thus it is said in the *Uttara*:

4a) He whose [mantra] is accumulated with *paurṇeśa* on the head, O Lord, would have the head and the crest-lock (*śikhā*); he whose [mantra] has *siddhaśa* as the calf-eye, the moon-rays as the eye, and *astra* as the glorious Bhairava and others— he is this one who dwells in the womb of Śrī.

The mantras belonging to the group of the supreme lords of supreme Śiva are of the form of the syllable *oṃ*; they, beginning with *ha-sa-kha-pa-ha*, are victorious as the eternal vision. In the nature of Śiva, because it ends in the *visarga*, it is called the power (*śakti*) of the letter *ra*.
Therefore, O Illustrious One, both Śiva and Parāśakti are all-pervasive. Thus it is said in the *Uttara-śaṅketaka*:
"They revolve, having drawn forth Śakti. Therefore, [I address] Śiva. By the word [Śiva], Parāśakti is the primary [meaning];
thus, "Salutation be to You! Salutation be to You!"—I offer my salutation. To whom? To Mahāmāyā. Thus [it is said].
This is the lunar procedure preceded by four syllables.
4b) Mahāmāyā pervades the world by means of the four syllables. She exists in a subtle state in the form of wind;
yet she is not within the range of vision, for she remains hidden in a non-dual state, situated within the navel.
In its gross form, it consists of four syllables: ya-ra-la-va; these are the powers of Will, Knowledge, Action, and the Pervasive Power (Vyāpinī).
Earth, water, fire, air, and space united; smell, touch, form, and sound;
time, knowledge, illusion, speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals; the resonance (nāda), the point (bindu), Śiva, and Śakti;
the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas; Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—[all these] are victorious.
Sadāśiva is white, red, yellow, and black; he is the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra;
he is the east, south, west, and north.

5a) The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages correspond to the rites of pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśya), and the malevolent rite (abhicāra). Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka),
and retention (kumbhaka) are associated with the heart, throat, navel, and genitals respectively.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! Paurṇamāsī, Niśākujā, Kālī, Mahāmāyā—these are the four days in the Āmnāya.
Māhāmāyā, through the four syllables, is full of bliss; she is the bestower of boons, whose nature is the letter A.
Māhārā is the form of the Mistress of the South (Dakṣiṇeśī). She is [denoted] by the group of letters beginning with *m*. She is the path of action (*karmamārga*) in well-performed deeds.

She is the goddess of the northern direction (*saumyadik*), the bestower of liberation. Furthermore, she is twofold: Māhā and Māsmā, that is, Mahāmāyā. She is Śiva and Śakti; she is destruction and creation, the sun, the moon, fire, wind, and the white [light].
Kṛṣṇa.
5b) White and red; night and day; below; above; the *haṃsa*; upward breath; *namaḥ*.
Unmanas, Meru, Mandara, Āli, Kāli, Māṃsa, Rakta, Ākāśa, Pṛthvī,
Liṅga, Vaidika, Bhairava, Pīṭhi, Brahmarandhra, Upastha, Bhūta, Bhaviṣya, Krūra, Saumya, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Uttarāyaṇa, and Dakṣiṇāyana.

Nature (prakṛti) is the Puruṣa; wisdom (prajñā) is the Baudhyarāha; skillful means (upāya) is the Saumyatā Aruṇā. This beginning and end is that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) of the Goddess, and she is indeed the Great Illusion. How is it that for a being in saṃsāra, this is exceedingly like an illusion? First of all, there are seeds, which have emptiness (śūnyatā) as their essence of gnosis (jñāna).

In the seedless state, Śiva and Śakti, through the state of aesthetic unification (*samarasībhāva*), give rise to the seeds. This is the sixfold method of the seed. From that, the maternal side [arises].
And the paternal side is sixfold, as is seen: bone, blood, and semen are the paternal side; flesh, blood, and skin are the maternal side; and the marrow.
The seed-mass will arise from the equal blending of the mother's side and the father's side.

And for ten months, through its conjunction, it grows. In the third month, it becomes solid; in the fourth month, it becomes an embryo (*aṅkura*). In the fifth month, the bones, skin, flesh, limbs, and minor members, as well as the mouth and nose, are produced. In the sixth month, it becomes endowed with consciousness (*cetanāvanta*). Then, seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) arise.
It occurs. These constitute the primary three channels within the channel; likewise:

6b) Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā. Iḍā carries [the breath] on the left, Piṅgalā carries it on the right, and Suṣumnā carries it in the middle. [These carry] blood, urine, and semen. By means of blood one becomes female, by means of semen one becomes male; through the equalization of these two, [neutrality arises].

The neuter [state]. Therefore, having known the channels (*nāḍī*) of woman and man, that which arises by their own will—of these two, the three channels, through the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), becoming a single channel, descend into the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); she is the Goddess Mahāmāyā. Having extended [the channels] individually and separately into the aperture of Brahmā, [they enter] the head, the chest, the palm of the hand, and the neck.

From the sides, the heart, the navel, the thighs, the knees, and the soles of the feet, and again from the navel, it becomes endowed with all splendor. Afterwards, as the *haṃsa* in the form of one's own breath, it moves upward by means of its movement.

7a) The downward flow occurs in the form of three channels: on the left is the female channel (*strī-nāḍī*), which carries the menstrual blood (*rajas*); on the right is the empty channel (*śūnya-nāḍī*), which carries the semen (*śukra*);

and in the middle, at the "beak of the bird" (*khagamukha*), is the male channel (*puruṣa-nāḍī*), which carries the semen. In the state of the equal flavor (*samarasa*) of woman and man, there is no [distinction].

It occurs; immediately thereafter, volition arises. Subsequently, there is the recollection of all previous births. Then, one is born into another birth. There is the pressure of the womb, painful sensation, and subsequently, the loss of mindfulness occurs.
Afterwards, there is the stage of childhood; there is the stage of youth; there is the stage of adolescence.
Therefore, she is Mahāmāyā. Immediately following that is the state of death; it is divided into two paths to nirvāṇa.

"And how is it twofold? [He replied: "Rebirth is not rebirth; it is of two kinds. By the grace of the feet of the true Guru, they know [it] through the distinction between the *dvādaśānta* and the *ṣoḍaśānta*."

7b) At the end of the twelve is the moon; at the end of the sixteen is the sun. O knower of the application of the petals, the twelve [fingers] ending with the moon are the *varaṇā* and *aṅguṣṭha*, reaching to the end of the *bindu*. This is the "moon yoga. And the cruel one is *koreka*.
Thus is the end of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*). Again, he speaks of the end of the sixteen-finger space (*ṣoḍaśānta*):

"Above the *bindu*, the *rudra* [space], and likewise the head (*śīrṣa*), which is above Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, there are four finger-breadths; above that, the sheath of power (*śaktikoṣṭa*) is proclaimed. Within those four finger-breadths, the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*) enters; then rebirth occurs."

One enters the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) and is not born again. When a triangle is formed at the end of the sixteen [fingers], there is the moon in the left corner, fire in the right corner, and the sun in the middle corner. Through the opening of the *śaṅkhinī*, these three orbs merge in a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*). By that means, one attains the desired goal and is not born again.

She herself is Mahāmāyā. [She is] the many scriptures such as the Vedas and grammar, the hundreds of meters (chandas), the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Nirukta, Jyotiṣa, Śikṣā, Kalpasūtras, and the Pañcarātra itself.

The followers of the six systems of philosophy (ṣaḍ-darśana) are: the Cārvāka, the Śaiva, the Vaiṣṇava, the Kṣapaṇaka, the Buddhist, and the Mīmāṃsaka who studies the Pātañjala [Yoga]. There are ninety-six heretical sects (pāṣaṇḍa) and eighteen great vows (mahāvrata). These are classified as pure (śuddha), mixed (saṃkīrṇa), and [the Śālāṅga].

There are four kinds of musical instruments: stringed (*tata*), percussion (*ānaddha*), solid (*ghana*), and wind (*sukhila*). It should be stated that there are four types: the stringed consists of lutes and the like; the percussion consists of drums such as the *muraja* and the like; the solid consists of cymbals, flutes, and the like; and the wind consists of flutes, reeds, and the like. Stringed music is of nine kinds; percussion consists of drums and the like; the solid...
The ninefold dance, beginning with cymbals and the like, is joyful;
it consists of the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, and the terrifying.

The loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful—thus are they established in many scriptures and other sources. There are sixteen vowels and thirty-three consonants; these forty-nine letters are pervaded by that Mahāmāyā.

The fifty-syllabled [mantra] ends with the letter *kṣa*; it consists of fifty spokes and is full. Having bowed to Mahāmāyā, who is joined with the *vaṃ* and *kaṣa*, she is that Mahāmāyā who, having abandoned the cause of emission (*visarga*), exists as pure being.

They possess the essential nature of Pradhāna. For it is said: "The origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds, as well as all fourfold classes of living beings—those born from a womb, those born from sweat, and those born from an egg—these are governed by her; she is Mahāmāyā, the pervader of the fourteen worlds comprising the entire triple-world. [The fourteen worlds:]... [The text continues with the enumeration of the fourteen worlds.]

The world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the great world (maharloka), the world of passion (janaloka), the world of austerity (tapoloka), the self-luminous world (svarloka), the world of truth (satyaloka); [and the subterranean realms:
Sutala, Nitala, Vitala, Talātala, Rasātala, and Pātāla.
These fourteen worlds are pervaded by you; O Mahāmāyā, salutations to you! This prostration is performed with my ten fingers and head, offered at your feet. Salutations! Salutations!

The subtle body is both supreme and non-supreme; it is the object of perception for the subtle and stainless [consciousness]. When the mind has transcended both the supreme and the non-supreme, it becomes equanimous (samarasībhūta) in the Supreme itself; that which does not perish by its own nature is the "supreme-non-supreme" of the Supreme Self. Likewise, it is the New Moon (Amāvāsyā), which, like the lion's glance, is the supreme face of the horse, manifold and facing outward.
The letter *na* is [represented by] a serpent, a skull, a staff, a vessel, a full moon, a trident, and other held weapons;
it is associated with the Yugas, the Vedas, the thunderbolt, Indra, Brahmā, and Hari. Rudra, together with his attendants, is the letter *ha*.

Victorious is that Kālī, who ends with Time (Kāla) and whose seat is Śiva; she who ends with dissolution (Laya) is pure and is said to be subtler than the subtle within the body. How is she colored by various states? For scripture after scripture speaks of her in many ways.

The *śikhā* [mantra] is colored by the *nāda*, *bindu*, and the letter *ha*, and by another [the letter *kṣa*]. Some are colored during exhalation (*recaka*), some during inhalation (*pūraka*), and some during retention (*kumbhaka*). Some are devoted to the ten-syllable [mantra]; some practice that *haṃsa*; some meditate on the void (*śūnya*).
Some are devoted to the *parākrama* [mantra], some to the *prāsāda*, and some are colored [by these].
Some are on the left and some on the right; some are in the middle and some are colored red.
Some are attached to the twenty-five principles, some are attached to the tip of a hair;
some are attached to the shadow in a person, and some are attached to sound.
Some are devoted to the resonance within the throat, while others are delighted by the soundless state.
Some, delighting in the upper path, [are situated] at the palate and the throat.

10a) Some are not colored by passion; some delight in dharma and adharma; the lowest of men feed on exhalations and inhalations. Some delight in the lotuses of the heart, while others are not colored by the lotuses of the navel. [They are proficient] in grammar, prosody, mathematics, and various other sciences.
He delighted in Nirukta, the Kalpasūtra, and the six systems of philosophy; he was devoted to the works of Dadhīci and Vālmīki, and he embraced the doctrine of dualism (Bhedavāda) in the Saṃgraha.
The Veda, grammar, prosody, as well as the Śatapatha [Brāhmaṇa], etymology, astronomy, and likewise the Kalpasūtras.
Likewise, others are devoted to the Pañcarātra, and similarly to the Buddhist and Ārhata systems;
others are devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga, while some are enamored with the Gāruḍa.
In the exposition of the meaning of songs and mantras, and in the introduction of other texts;
and furthermore, in the case of designations, the syllable is the form of the practitioner of mantra.
And others, having reflected upon the texts, are practitioners of mantra whose form is the syllable;
they are great illusions, who are delighted at heart with joy.
10b) Those men who have destroyed the differentiation of powers do not attain liberation for him;
these are the gross ones of great illusion, whose minds are delighted by worldly pleasures.
Men do not attain liberation for him without the piercing of the *śakti*;
therefore, one should always practice that path of *śakti* with diligent effort.
Just as a row of birds staying in the sky is not bound by anyone, so too one who is liberated is not slain;
yet those who are bound by the snare of craving fall upon the surface of the earth.
For in this way the self is slain, deluded by the net of illusion;
the great snare of the net of illusion is indeed the retinue of Śiva.
Such being the state of the world, what is the use of those possessed of but a fraction [of knowledge]? Knowledge is considered by the wise to be that which brings about the welfare of all;

and when all arts and sciences are combined together, each person appropriates his own portion and becomes absorbed in it, just as the female bee first offers her own seat upon the letter *ra* and then settles there.
The division is six; in the moon of the vowels, the void (kha) is called the great seed-syllable of the body.
"Solitary and pure in self, she is the one called Nāda, garlanded with points (bindu). Thus it is said.
In the axle of sound, in the locus of sound, in the three locations—the throat, the hollow of the chest, and the heart—at the navel, [one perceives] the sequence beginning with the Ṛgveda.
There are twenty-one modulations (*mūrcchanās*). These follow a sequence of seven;

thus, modulation (*amūrcchaṇā*) has three locations: the navel, the heart, and the throat. It follows the sequence of the *ṛg* verses and possesses resonance in these three locations. The *Bindumālinī* is the state at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta-pada*), consisting of the moon, sun, and fire. Because one follows [the breath] by means of that, it is called *Bindumālinī*. It is also termed the "Stream of Nectar" (*amṛtadhārā*).

The solitary power (*śakti*) is that by which the man is known as one who has been pierced by power. He who possesses the power to restrain the five senses has the seed of power (*śaktibīja*). And this [seed] is solitary and heated.
By that person for whom purity arises, one knows the differentiation of the powers;
that is, the person whose mind becomes steady.

For him, there is the attainment of the garland of drops (*bindumāli*). He is joined with the form of yoga. There are fires for the yogī-sesame; in the mind, the urine is slight, and the impurity is consumed without agitation. This is the first sign. And so it is said in the *Uttara*:

"Ekashakti is called 'the Mountain' (naga) and is pure by virtue of its nature as the Bindu; Malini, on the other hand, is the all-pervading [power] by virtue of its nature as the Nada. Thus it is said.
When the state beyond the body has arisen, one is devoid of the body; at the end of the body, there exists that which is bodiless.

At the end of the body, within the triangular seat (*pīṭha*) shaped like the syllable *aiṃ*, there is the bodiless lotus-shaped hexagon and quadrangle, the ocean, the riverbank, and Devīkoṭa; it exists within the lotus inside the triangle—that is the Bodiless One (*adehā*). She is Consciousness (*vijñānā*). Thus.

The pervasion of Śiva, which previously existed as the movement of the serpent [of power] within the body, is established as non-dual; it neither arises nor perishes, being established like the ether.

12a) *Acalā* is the sustainer of the universe. It is called *acala* because it does not move. Through gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, by this procedure, the stability of the body of an unmoving person is maintained, or [it is maintained] at the time of the destruction of the body.
The dual consciousness does not undergo destruction; she is the sustainer of the universe. Because she assumes many forms, she is the Sustainer (Vidhāriṇī).
How are earth, water, wind, fire, moon, sun, and space its form?
The Brāhmaṇīs and others are her yoginīs; thirty-three crores of gods constitute her form.

The syllable Oṃ, the syllable Namaḥ, the syllable Svāhā, the syllable Svadhā, the syllable Vauṣaṭ, the syllable Vaṣaṭ, the syllable Hūṃ, and the syllable Aiṃ—these are the birth-mantras (jāti-mantra) from which its very origin arises. The Bhairavas, such as Asitāṅga and others, are its forms; their origin occurs through its locus. [This is] the body, speech, mind, and intellect.
Passion, hatred, anger, greed, delusion, and malice are observed to have arisen.
12b) Therefore, [she is called] "the Sustainer of the Universe. Likewise on the right: She is the Immovable All-Knowing One; she is not formless, yet she abides within all bodies.
Indeed, the Eternal One who sustains the universe is neither gentle nor of empty form.

The Great Kuṇḍalinī is eternal. She is situated in the center of the navel in the form of a coil. She is the crooked ornament of the Lord of Serpents, appearing in the playful form of the Lord of Elephants. Within the center of the navel, this Kuṇḍalinī moves both upward and downward. Moving upward, she pervades the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) between the moon and the sun. Downward...

The attainment of the state where power has departed [is reached] at the two thighs, within the central channel (nāḍī), and likewise in the north. That by which the five knots are to be pierced dissolves upward into Śiva; it is known as the Great Sound (mahāśabda). Having endured [the practice], let the three fluids be held. One should avoid the young girl, the one with a mouth full of saliva, the eunuch, and the one who is emaciated.
There, the tree is split open and adorned with the crescent moon; it is the supreme body, sustained by the mantra of Mahākuṇḍalinī.

13a) Situated in the midst of the *haṃsa*, she abides in the form of an upward-moving *haṃsa*. The movement of the breath is the movement of the *haṃsa*; it has a single meaning: the upward breath (*ūrddha-śvāsa*). The downward breath (*adhaḥ-śvāsa*) is twofold. [The first is] upward...

The exhalation is the *ahaṃkāra*. The downward breath is *saḥ*; it is the *tārā*. By that, the *haṃsa* is expressed. Moving downward in the form of semen (*śukra*), it brings about the expansion of living beings. Moving upward, it is established in the middle of the fire-wood (*tāmīdhe*). It is called the *kuṇḍalinī*. The *haṃsa* is both creation and dissolution. Śiva and Śakti exist in a dual form.
It has a dual form; she is situated in the midst of the *haṃsa*. Thus it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
The downward breath as well as the upward breath, moving in the middle, becomes the *madhyamā*; she is Śiva and Śakti by nature, the cause of both creation and dissolution.
Abiding in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire, he pervades the void, both supreme and non-supreme.
13b) Soma, Sūrya, and Agni are situated therein. [The channels] Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā correspond to Soma, Sūrya, and Agni respectively.
Fire is in the place of water; wind is in the middle of the place of fire. Situated in this middle is the center of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni.
She has gone.

"Pervading the sky, supreme and non-supreme" means the upward-moving breath. Situated at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), in the location of the "end of twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) and the "end of sixteen" (*ṣoḍaśānta*), the moon dissolves into the sun and fire when they have become one in essence; thus it pervades the sky.
Between the supreme and the non-supreme, and in the movement within that [breath], she remains established in the form of the Transmental (*unmanā*), dissolved into the Void (*śūnya*).
In the subtle form of the supreme and the subordinate, those situated in the middle [should practice] with downward breath;

having mastered the pure, peaceful *sivādi* sound submerged in the fire, well-united with the sun, within the mantra of the sky— namely *kha*, moon, fire, and sun— one should perform meditation upon that slender form in the heart, the supreme navel, and the middle.
"Manifested in three ways,
it is known through speech and cognition"— thus one should contemplate the mantras daily at the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā). And so it is said in the Uttara [Tantra]:
The supreme Śakti is Nābhāśāntā, and the supreme Śiva is Nāmāvāsyā; I consider the mantra of these two to be the bestower of the boons of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

In the state of the embodiment of the syllable *oṃ*: the syllable *oṃ* consists of three deities. *O* is Brahmā, *nāda* (the resonance) is Viṣṇu, and the *bindu* (dot) is Maheśvara and Śiva. *U* is Śakti, and *a* is Śiva; these three, having become one in essence, constitute the syllable *oṃ*. That *oṃ* is Mahāmāyā. The embodiment of *oṃ* is the curved form (*kuṭilākā*), moving upwards.
And thus, in the Bhairavatantra, it says: "The downward movement."
The syllable Oṃ is the supreme mantra; it is also called the seed-syllable of Śiva. The syllable Oṃ is the universe itself, all-pervading, the Lord, and omnipresent.
The bearer of half of half of the letter *ha*. The letter *ha*. The bearer of half. Half of the letter *ha*. *ti* (the syllable *ti*). Half of the letter *ha*.
The half of the letter *ha* has become a drop (*bindu*).
It is said to have the form of a half-moon and a womb (*yoni*). The half of the letter *ha* and the half of the letter *ṭha* constitute the word; it is without syllables (*nirakṣara*).

It is called the "footstep" (*pada*). How can a footstep that is without syllables, beyond the path of speech, and outside the range of perception be seen? Those deluded do not see it with the foremost of their eyes; they do not understand the non-conceptual, yet they pursue conceptualization. They think of it as stainless, yet they perceive it as stained; they contemplate it, yet they do not realize it; they worship it, yet they do not see it.
By which one sees that which is situated within oneself as being whirled about, even though it is immovable.
While meditating, one does not see; while awakening, one does not awaken. Inference and direct perception are like the mind with respect to that which is immeasurable.
They treat what is not a proper place as a vessel; they purify what is already perfectly pure.
They perform what is not an action as an action; they turn non-duality into duality.
They practice the non-conduct while cultivating the state of non-existence; they conceptualize coming and going, though it is devoid of both coming and going.
15a) They conceptualize non-differentiation as differentiation, though it is devoid of extremes and sides;
it is all-pervading and unified, yet one should enter that which stands at the pinnacle, far beyond.
They accomplish the changeless, which is both supreme and non-supreme, by means of the form of change;
they accomplish that which is both sound and non-sound, yet is devoid of both sound and non-sound.
Though it is being explained, they do not understand, for no [logical] position is perceived;
yet they do not desist from reciting, like those who are mute, blind, and deaf.
They do not conceptualize what is directly perceived, nor do they understand while listening;
alas, through the nectar-like teaching, they release themselves from the bonds of delusion.
Just as a worm in a boil knows neither bondage nor liberation, so do parents act toward their son with beneficial intent, as if he were immortal.
Like moths [flying] into a fire, they desire their own downfall;
how could there be liberation for those whose minds are enslaved by sense objects?
And there, the hunter perceives the flavors through his destruction; others merely seek after material things, like an intellect that is declining.
At the time of death there is despair; at the hour of the end, it is like poison. Just as toward a departed friend, the mind feels a sense of loss.
When struck, it brings about pain; likewise, when encountered as a sense object, it does so;
yet when honored by friends and attended to, it brings happiness.
Just as those who desire the news of some delicious taste act toward their instruments, so too does the arrogant one,
puffed up with pride in his own self, act on account of his own conceptual constructions.
O Vṛhaspati, what is the use of grammar for one who is full of pride?
Those who possess no letters [of learning] always practice grammar until it reaches exhaustion.
Good conduct is devoid of color and free from the characteristics of sound;
it is colorless, present in all places, beyond qualities, and beyond the sphere of sensory perception.
Inexpressible and free from material elements, it is difficult to attain through mere practice;
though situated within the body, it remains distant from the knowledge of the world.
Free from merit and demerit, eternal, and the essence of the assembly of bliss,
it resides within the bodies of the foremost among gods, asuras, and humans.
But that [distinction] is difficult for those of small intellect to discern, such as the differentiation between them.
And what does he do in the treatises? He is directly perceived by the guardians of the earth; he has been fashioned by sages, gods, humans, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Even those beginning with Brahmā, who are thinkers on the scriptures, are all completely liberated by that;
for that reason, the state of the words of the Indestructible is always established.
For that reason, having meditated upon the syllable and the word:
"O Lakṣmīkaṇṭha, O Mahāsena, whose seat is the fire-peak."
And with the twelfth [vowel], it is conjoined with the cruel [letter] Khaṇḍendu;
this is the seed-syllable for the concentration of the mind. And so it is said in the Uttara:
They go from Brahmā to the Imperishable (akṣara), and beyond the Imperishable to Śiva;
the Supreme God is the abode of liberation, and the Great Goddess is Mahāmāyā.
Thus it is said.

In that which is as subtle as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, infinite, inexhaustible, and imperishable—(16b) "hair" (*vāla*) means a lock of hair; "a hundredth part of the tip of a hair" (*vālāgra-śatadhā-bheda*); "infinite" (*ananta*) means it has no measure, being immeasurable.

It is subtle, not seen even when divided a hundredfold like the tip of a hair; it is infinite, inexhaustible, and immutable. Of that which exists, there are thousands; even though birth and death occur, there is no destruction. And so it is said in the Uttara-tantra: "The yogi, through meditation upon the wheel of qualities beginning with omniscience, attains the Supreme Self through its attributes; he who has gone beyond the left, the Kula, and the non-Kula is supreme."
I bow to the manifestations of the nature of emptiness, which bestow happiness and grant supreme bliss.
In the support of the half-measure of the letter Ha.

17a) Resting upon the filaments of the lotus (*padma-kiñjalka*). The support is the filaments; it is shaped like a lotus. The three [lotuses] are situated in the secret place, hidden within the lotus, resting upon the power (*śakti*). The lotus is triangular. [The stages of] arising and destruction.
The place.
That supreme Bhṛgu, together with the letter *repha*, [forms] *ku* and *ṭa*; likewise, having pierced the sky (*na*) and the fourteenth vowel (*au*), the seed-syllable is said to be brought forth.
The seed-syllable for the protection of the body is JÑĀḤ; likewise, it is in the south at night.
The abiding, arising, and withdrawing of the Great Goddess are supported by the lotus.
Established in the left-hand path, she is Mahāmāyā, the enchanting one. Thus it is said.
O you who are enriched by all things, O Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), O Giver of Boons, O you who are worshipped by the world!

She is called "Lokapūjitā" because she is worshipped by the worlds. Without the Goddess Mahāmāyā, there is no origination, maintenance, or dissolution of the worlds; for that reason, she is worshipped by the world. Thus it is said.

17b) "Named Sakalā" means accompanied by *kalā*; *kalā* refers to the thirty-eight *kalās*. O Mahāmāyā, you who are exceedingly like an illusion (*māyopamā*) and have arisen from the science of all mechanical devices (*yantra-śāstra*), therefore you are Mahāmāyā in that state. O Granter of Boons, you are desired by the world.

She is the giver of fruits; likewise, she is Mahāmāyā in her primordial form, the bestower of boons and the giver of fearlessness. She is the very nature of Śakti, the all-conquering, the supreme, and the transcendent. She is the female consort (mudrā), the mother of the one whose banner is the hand (the Elephant-headed God), and the bestower of peace from all afflictions. Those fools of wicked intellect, the barbarians who seek only fruits, perceive her in that [limited] way.
Having struck them down, the fire of non-dual compassion has shaved some bald, made others wear five tufts of hair, turned others into matted-haired ascetics,
and others still into Kāpālikas.
Each individual channel (*nāḍī*) pierces one vital point (*marman*) situated in its center;
each channel is the Suṣumṇā, which, through the division of its ashes, is seen as seventy-two thousand channels.
In the form of the Suṣumṇā, it flows through the body. There are thirty-eight vital points; their piercing constitutes life. These are the vital points.

There is no death by piercing [the channels] at a time when one is endowed with *kāla* (the power of Time). Therefore, she pierces each vital point (*marman*) by her own nature. Likewise, through the right channel, she is the goddess whose form is auspiciously radiant, bestowing the knowledge of Yoga.
At the end of the delusion, she is of the nature of power; she is one and yet of manifold forms.
O Goddess, the thirty-eight-fold *kalā* is the piercer in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
O Lord, she whose nature consists of the thirty-eight *kalās* is the pervasive Nāḍī within the five faces of the Goddess; she is Mahāmāyā, my own delusion. Thus are the thirty-eight *kalās*.
Śvaśinī, Maṅgadā, Ariṣṭā, Marīci, Jvālinī, as well as Pravṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā; these are the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas in their extensive forms.
Delusion is darkness, ignorance is exhaustion, sleep is disease, death is hunger, and thirst is [the heat of] passion.
Dust is attachment, blood is aversion, and the act of restraint is the protection against desire.
Vṛddhikārī, Rātrī, Bhramanī, Bhrāmanī, Jvarā, Siddhi,
Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kāsthī, Prajā, and Svadhā.
Among these thirty-eight *kalās*, *Bhedinī* resides in all living beings;
likewise, *Aśvinī* is the breath (*śvāsa*), *Aṅgadā* is the body (*śarīra*), *Iṣṭā* is the modification of the mind (*cittavikāra*), and *Marīci* is the rays (*raśmi*).
Jvalinī is the crest-lock (śikhā), the light (jyotis). Nivṛtti is the state free from modification (nirvikāra). Pratiṣṭhā is well-established attainment; Vidyā is the manifold tradition (āgama).
The Vedas, the four auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyā).
Action leads to heaven and liberation, as well as accomplishment, supernatural power, and the possession of knowledge; thus the Āgama is said to be supreme.
19a) One hundred thousand [verses] for this science of grammar (*śabda-śāstra*), and four hundred thousand for astronomy (*jyotiṣa*); these are the branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Peace (*śānti*) is the pacification; darkness (*stamaḥ*) is the person of time (*kāla-puruṣa*); delusion (*moha*) resides in the five senses; decay (*kṣaya*) is destruction; sleep (*nidrā*).
Impurity; illness; disease; death; dying; hunger; thirst.
*Prasiddhaḥ* (well-known). *Stṛṣā* (thirst). *Pipāsā* (thirst). *Rajaḥ* (dust). *Puṣpamāsikā* (the month of flowers). *Rakṣaḥ* (a demon). *Prasiddhaḥ* (well-known). *Ratiḥ* (pleasure).
Sexual intercourse; the one to be protected; the nourisher; sensual desires; specific tasks; and the woman as well as sexual union.

Restraint; forbearance; action; that which is to be done; the aged; increasing; the non-performer of duty; distinction; night; steady; night-wandering; roaming; wandering; deluding; excited; fever; envy; accomplishment;
the [eight] powers beginning with atomization (animā); minor; prosperity; strength; splendor; renown; brilliance; fortune.
It is well known: *medhā* is intelligence (*buddhi*).
19b) Lustre, Splendor, Progeny, Origination, Nourishment, and Withdrawal— these are the thirty-eight digits (kalās).
By this division of *kalās*, [the power] pierces that which has reached the *brahmarandhra*. By this division of *kalās*, one should withdraw [the breath]. How?

Into the division at the *brahmarandhra*—that is, through the gate of Brahmā (*brahmadvāra*). The moon, sun, and fire, having become equal, cause the *mṛta-kuṇḍalinī* to expand; one should flood all the limbs with nectar. For that reason, it is called "piercing" (*bhedinī*) at the *brahmarandhra*.

It is said: Furthermore, there are thirty-eight digits (*kalā*). There are ten digits of Agni, twelve digits of Sūrya, and sixteen digits of Candra. Again, he speaks of the specific digits of Agni: Prāṇa, Apāna, and Vyāna.
Udāna, Samāna, Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
Regarding their locations within the body: it is not stated [explicitly], but the *prāṇa* is in the heart; the *apāna* is in the anus (*guḍa*).
The *samāna* [wind] is in the navel-center; the *udāna* is in the region of the throat; and the *vyāna* belongs to all embodied beings.
Furthermore: The *nāga* wind should be known to reside in the heart; the *kūrma* wind is situated in the opening of the eyes; the *kṛkara* wind is in the eyes;
and the *devadatta* wind is in yawning. The *dhanañjaya* wind does not leave even when one is dead.
The aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the navel, the bladder, and the anus— these are the digits of the Sun (sūryakalā).
Skin, flesh, blood, marrow, fat, sinew, bone, semen, mind, intellect, passion, hatred,
delusion, anger, and sorrow— these are the sixteen digits of the moon.

These digits (kalās) pervade the body. For that reason, the Goddess, consisting of thirty-eight digits, is the divider within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhraka). This is the procedure for the aperture of Brahmā and the heart: [it involves] emanation, withdrawal, and the great withdrawal.

20b) By piercing that *brahmarandhra*, one attains immortality and liberation (*mokṣa*). For that reason, [the practice] should not be performed by means of the two *brahmarandhras*. Within the womb, in the center of the corner, the fire blazes.
The smokeless flame: within that, the vital wind consumes the mass of the living soul; for that reason.

A hot wind blows at that time of death; consequently, the fire is extinguished, and because of that, the wind becomes cold. For that reason, when the fire has diminished, it should be increased through the practice of yoga or by means of karma. One should consume little food. From the diminution of the fire, wind-disease arises; from the increase of the fire, bile-disease arises.
Having made the moon, sun, and fire equal in intensity above the Brahma-aperture at the crown of the head, one should cause [the breath] to be severed by that [force] and flood [the body].
This is done within the fire and the life-mass (*jīvapiṇḍa*). How is it known how to make the moon, sun, and fire equal?
21a) Many scriptural traditions have been observed by Avalokita through the three samayas that are pure in the lineage of the gurus.
Through the restraint of body, speech, and mind, [the goal] is attained; it is not through the study of scriptures, mantras, or vidyās, for [it] is devoid of parts and sub-parts.
O Karṇa, by the grace of the Guru's feet, this has indeed been realized:
the sun dissolves into fire, and the moon dissolves into the sun.
This remains in the state of equal flavor (samarasa), established in the form of space;
in the midst of that, one should flood [the mind] with the transcendent, utterly severed from the vital breaths and so forth.
"By that very application, she who pierces [the knots] resides in the aperture of Brahmā. Thus it is said.
Lākula is the crest of the fire; Bhānu is the long flame;
Vibhu is the moon; Anala is the sound; Khaṇḍendu is the drop (bindu); and Tatkalā is the digit (kalā).
The Tantra of the Preservation of the Seed-Syllables of the Thirty-Eight Kalās. And so it is said in the Uttara:
Just as with the gods, so too with the goddesses in the purification of the elements;
one should contemplate them at the end of the *śuklirā* as the all-pervading power (*vyāpi-śakti*).
21b) "The Brahman-weapon that pierces."
The goddess resembles a flash of lightning, her form coiled like a serpent;
she is like a streak of lightning in the sky, a radiance of splendor.
It has no form like a reflected image, it is formless and devoid of materiality;
it is ineffable, non-existent, and beyond the range of speech.
Even with a thousand attempts at violent exertion, his form cannot be found.

It is known through the instruction of the true guru; for that reason, it is called the "lightning-creeper" (*vidyullatā*). It resembles lightning; its color is like lightning. Its color is unknowable: it is not white, not red, not yellow, not black, not green, not emerald-green, not the color of a lotus, nor is it variegated. And that is the color of the lightning-creeper.
The color of lightning is obtained. The form of a serpent is crooked; "serpent" refers to snakes, whose form is crooked. The movement of a wheel is like that of an arm.
22a) *Kuṭilākṛtiḥ* refers to the goddess; *kuṭilakuṇḍalinī* means she who possesses curved earrings, that is to say, *amṛtakuṇḍalinī*.
The crooked form of the seven lords of serpents, though curved, is a beautiful line established through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

In the center of the heart is Kuṇḍalinī; there the power of Nāda dissolves. She is established within the midst of the bodies of all moving and unmoving things—the three worlds and the fourteen realms of existence. That Goddess Mahāmāyā has the form of a serpent’s coil, she in whom Śiva and Śakti have become one in equal flavor (samarasa).

That Mahāmāyā of the Goddess is differentiated by means of differentiation, yet she does not exist as anything separate; her essential nature is non-dual. When known, she is the great liberation. Thus it is said in the Bhāsā: "Her form is like the brilliance of lightning, appearing as a radiant light that pervades all."
With a jewel garland coiled like a serpent held in her royal hand,
she is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These are the five great pretas.
One should serve the feet of Mahāmāyā, which have been touched by his crown.

These five great pretas are stationed at the feet of that fivefold deity; the meaning is that these great pretas are eternally served at the base of the goddess's feet. That [deity] consists of the five deities: speech, mind, intellect, and ego.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, odor, taste, touch, and sound.
Niyati (Destiny), Kāla (Time), Rāga (Attachment), Vidyās (Knowledge), Māyās (Illusion), Vāk (Speech), Pāṇi (Hand), Pāda (Foot), and Pāyu (Excretory Organ).

Pasthāḥ, Nandāḥ, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, Pūrṇā; Bālā, Kumārī, Yuvatī, Sthavirā, Ānandā, Karī, Uditā, Bhramitā, Sadhyā, Astā. Accompanied by these [times], one should approach the base of the Goddess’s feet. Specifically, at the base of the feet (aṅghrimūla), which is the gateway to the ends of the body.
23a) From that, moreover, specific qualities arise, as do specific qualities of wind.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Or rather, these two are said to be the established positions: the base of the foot and the base of the nose. These two are pervaded by the vital air (vāyu).
Established in the right and left nostrils, she is Mahāmāyā, the Supreme; [she resides] below and above.

Transversely in the middle, [the breath] is established; the prāṇa-vāyu flows. Eighteen vikalās and four prāṇas flow in the earth-position; the Āditya [node], the lips, and the heart [are involved]. In the Māhendra-yoga, during the Leo transit, a duration of twelve aṅgulis flows. The apāna-vāyu flows for seventy-five vikalās and three [prāṇas].
Prāṇa is the station of water; it is the rising of Saturn, a beautiful conjunction, the transition into Virgo, and the four-fingered speech.
The Samāna wind flows for thirty-seven kalās; there are three prāṇas, the location of fire, and Mars is the age.
The death-yoga, the transition of the breath, and the statement of eight finger-breadths: the udāna wind flows.
Eighteen minutes [of arc] at the position of the Moon’s Pravāyu [node] indicate the rising of a kingdom; it is a portentous conjunction (*utpāta-yoga*).
The transition into Sagittarius (Dhanus): it carries the statement of eighteen finger-breadths; in the center, the Vyāna wind flows.
The yoga of the void consists of a single inhalation in the space of the sky.
At the transit of the sun into Libra (tulā-saṃkrānti), these [winds] flow through the right nostril; this is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) in the lower portion.
Cancer is obtained in the following left nostril-passage; the earth element is situated below, and the Naga-wind flows in the place of earth; it consists of eighteen vikalās and four prāṇas.
24a) The arising of the Buddha, the yoga of accomplishment; the transit of Aquarius; it carries the twelve-fingered statement.
The tortoise-wind flows; at seventy-five *vikalās*, it is the station of water, the rising of the moon, and the conjunction of nectar.
The transit of Pisces: the wind flows through four fingers; the *kṛka* wind flows; thirty-seven *kalās* and four *prāṇas*. In the locus of fire, there is the rising of Venus and the *śivayoga*.
The transit of Taurus. It carries a statement of eight finger-breadths. The wind blows for Devadatta. Eighteen *vikalās* and four *prāṇas*. The station of the wind. The *gaṇḍa* conjunction.

The transit of Gemini; the rising of Jupiter; it carries the statement of eight finger-breadths; in the middle, the wind blows as Dhananjaya; it is a single breath; the locus of space is the Śūla-yoga.
24b) The transit of Aries; the rising of Ketu. These belong to the left nostril. The northern solstice; the Capricorn [ascendant] above.
The upward-moving [breath] is the withdrawal; these three together constitute the movement of the breath.
The Māhendra-Vāyu breath flows; it consists of five kalās and three prāṇas, and is the Māhendra-yoga.
The transit of the lion; the pair of Śivas; the statement of eight finger-breadths; Agni carries the wind.
Seven vikalās; two prāṇas; belonging to Agni.
In the northeast (Māhendra) there is honor and worship; in the southeast (Āgneya) there is doubt regarding life;
in the northwest (Vāyavya) there is fear and disease; but in the west (Vāruṇa) there is the accomplishment of all goals.
Exhalation, inhalation, and retention are born of the vital air;
one who understands the sequence of the vital airs is one whose time for the perfection of yoga has arrived.
In that regard, he speaks again of the destruction of the breath: when it flows as a single movement through either the left or the right [nostril], then one is said to have reached death.
25a) When it moves as a single current for five days, if it flows for ten days, one lives for two years.
If it carries for one fortnight, it lives for one year; when it carries for twenty days, then it lives for three months.

In thirty-six [days], there is the transition of fire (*agni-saṃkrānti*) at three finger-breadths of yoga. Fire flows toward the northwest (*vāyavya*); it consists of five *vikalās* and five *prāṇas*.
The transition into Vāyavya. In the statement regarding the five fingers, the wind of the elephant (vāraṇa-vāyu) blows; it is sixty vikalās.

The sixfold breath, the auspicious conjunction, and the dissolution into Śiva—these three become of one flavor in the center. Within sixty-six finger-breadths, it brings about the arising of the sixteen transits; that day it sustains [the breath], and he lives for one season.
If it flows for twenty-seven days, he lives for one month; if it flows for twenty-eight days, he lives for one month; if it flows for twenty-eight days, he lives for one fortnight.
If it flows for nineteen days, he lives for ten years; if it flows for one month, he lives for five days;
if it flows for thirty-one days, he lives for three days; if it flows for thirty-two days...
When he lives for two days, he carries [the breath] for thirty-three days; when he lives for one day, he lives for two days.
In one day and night, there are one hundred thousand breaths; this is the movement of the breath.

One should recite the five mantras taught by the Supreme Lord—Śrīkaṇṭha, Krūra, Vidhu, Kurma, and Anantavaktra—which are employed against those agitated by the wrath of Ḍiṇḍika and others, as well as against enemies. One should recite them at times both regular and irregular; indeed, one should recite them when death is imminent or when fear seizes the ears. This should be done by one who is equanimous, in a solitary place, and has conquered the senses.

The movement of the breath is difficult for the common person to grasp; it is known by the common person only as the mere flow of breath. By this [knowledge], one has not understood the practice of food-restraint or the performance of actions such as meditation, which are beyond the reach of ordinary people.
"These five great pretas are stationed at the soles of his feet," thus [it is said].
Likewise, it is stated in the Kulākulārṇava:
The gods, beginning with Brahmā, are the cause; they have gone to the pair of feet of the Goddess.
Abiding in the form of a ghost, he exists as the very nature of Time for all.
O Goddess, Mother of the three worlds, salutations to you who are the embodiment of Śakti!
You are the Mother of the three worlds; in whose presence the origin of the world of the three realms occurs, therefore, O Compassionate One, you are the Mother of the three worlds.
"Mother" means one whose nature is that of a mother. You are established throughout the three worlds—both the moving and the unmoving beings.
That mother Mahāmāyā is the progenitor;
she is the birthplace, the eternal means for accomplishing the three worlds.
The accomplishment of all aims; the place where the essential meaning of the Samaya is spoken. In that manner, the mother is in the southern corner, which is heaven.

26b) In the left corner is the mortal realm; in the lower corner is the netherworld (pātāla). Thus, she is the mother of the three worlds. She is called Devī because she is the power (śakti) within the Divine (deva). And so it is stated in the *Kulārkapaṇṇaraka* and in the *Kālajñānapadmāṅkura* regarding the thirty-two syllables:

In the expansion of the root: the petals of the Goddess extend from the base to the tip; they are threefold in width and twofold at the edges. The filaments are arranged around the pericarp, five in number, resembling the five [elements]. In the lotus named Padma, there is a hollow cavity outside, extending from Kūrma to Śiva; it consists of eternal bliss, bestows the fruits of the month of Māgha, and has a single hair in its center.

"Salutation! My head has been rubbed against your feet; therefore, I offer my obeisance. Thus [he spoke]. The Mother is the one who brings about birth; she is Mahāmāyā, the eldest among children, possessing the nature of the three triads. Her manifestation as Brahmā occurred from the left cheek; she was born from the right cheek as Oṃkāra. [This is] the body and mind.
Having become one, [this is] the salutation.

27a) Thus, the purpose of the salutation is out of reverence. Śaktirūpiṇī is the state of being of the nature of power; Śiva is the one whose form is that power, established in a state of equal flavor (samarasa) through his form. She is Śaktirūpiṇī. There are three divisions of power: below, in the middle, and above.
Arrogance.
The *saṃpuṭa* [mantra] consists of five *praṇavas*, and the form of Kujā is known as ninefold;
this thirty-two-syllable mantra is heard to be the mother of the three worlds.
She is the supreme mantra among mantras, bestowing the fruit of all desires;
and so it is stated in the Uttara [Tantra].
The entire universe, both stationary and moving, rests within the support of Śakti;
Śakti creates and protects, and at the time of dissolution, she is Śivā, the bestower of liberation.
Situated between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, she has the form of a lotus fiber;

like a lotus fiber or a lotus stalk, that Mahāmāyā has the nature of a subtle thread. And it is said in the *Kulākulārṇava*: "Her movement proceeds through a succession of subtle stages, like a continuous string of very soft and extended lotus fibers."
She who possesses the pair of playful marks (līlāla),
who pierces the six cakras, and who pervades the interior of Akula, Kula, and Kulāntara— she alone is the Śakti in this world, the victorious one whose form is radiant splendor.

Śrī Kujeśī: This [central channel] has the form of a lotus fiber. Situated between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, it is called the triple-channel *suṣumnā*. *Iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* correspond to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; to the netherworld (*pātāla*), the mortal world (*martya*), and heaven (*svarga*);
to the moon, the sun, and fire; and to earth, water, and air; as well as to red, white, and heat.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas; the principle of the self (ātmatattva), the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva); creation, maintenance, and dissolution; Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī;
the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; the future; the present; the heart, the throat, and the palate;
*aḥ*, *uḥ*, and *maḥ*; *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*; Meru, Mandara, and Kailāsa.
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the Ocean; Dharma, Kāma, and Mokṣa—this is the distinction of the three channels (trināḍī).
Iḍā and Piṅgalā;
[and] Brahmā and Viṣṇu. In their midst, if there is a thread of the lotus stalk, it flows in the form of the equal taste (samavara), [carrying] the Moon.

"The streams are consumed by the fire of the sun. Likewise, at night: "The form situated between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* is like a lotus fiber; that goddess, who is the bliss of the world, is revealed to those joined in yoga as having the form of a lotus fiber."
The Goddess has entered into the center of the *bindu*; she is *kuṭilā* (the crooked one) and possesses the crescent moon (*ūrdhvacandrikā*).

The *bindu* is space; the *kuṭilā* has come through its center. Having reached the *kuṭilā*, she has descended. The half-moon is the form of the letter *ṭha*; it is like the shape of a half-moon at the heart and navel in the upper region, while the navel is in the lower region.

Within the womb (*yoni*), in that place within the lotus, is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). That womb is the half-moon, triangular in shape. The point (*bindu*) is established as the *liṅga* of space. Therefore, Śiva is of the nature of the point, and the half-moon is the form of Sound (*nāda*). Śiva and Śakti are the forms of Sound and Power (*śakti*).

28b) That which is half-formed is the crooked one (*kuṭila*). The *jīvapiṇḍa* is the crescent moon (*ardhacandra*). Having placed the first and last syllables, it is the devourer of the mother of Bhṛgu (the letter *i*). It is conjoined with the waning crescent moon (*khaṇḍendu*).
It illuminates the seed-syllable of the *bindu*. And so it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:

The Śakti has entered into the center of the Bindu; she is the Half-moon and the Nectar of the Crooked One (Kuṭilā), who has become the life-force of the world. "Salutations to you, O Liṅga-Śakti! She shines like a drop of frost, suspended at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta), and is the river of breath. *Tuṣārakanikā* means a drop of frost (*tuṣākanikā*), a drop of snow (*himakanikā*); it is a specific kind of *kanikā*. *Kanikā* [means a small particle].

The *bindu* means a drop of snow; like a particle of frost, that radiance follows along by way of the *dvādaśānta*, and being thus supported, that Great Māyā satisfies the Supreme Lord. And so it is said in the *Uttara*:
"Residing at the *dvādaśānta*, suspended from Kālarudra,
that goddess, the bliss of the universe, always bestows satisfaction."
Gaurī went to Umā’s peak with the splendor of twelve Ādityas;
her radiance was like that of the twelve Ādityas, possessing the brilliance of twelve suns.

"Umā resides within that body; she has entered the center of Unmanā. She is the cause, the Great Māyā, inconceivable, non-dual, and beyond the sphere of speech. "Gaurī has ascended to the peak of Unmāda. *U* and *Mā* constitute *Umā*, for *hi* signifies certainty. And thus it is shown in the *Vilīnottara*: "She has gone halfway. Her lotus-feet are worshipped by the three worlds.

In time, upon the head of Rudra-Agni, and likewise in the world of the two Yāmas, within the sphere of the perfected Brahmāṇḍa, she who bears the Khaṭvāṅga in her left arm and the excellent knife and the vessel of mantra in her right hand; she who is white, adorned with a loosened necklace, and who bows in heaven—I bow to Bhavā, the sustainer of the universe. Thus.
"By the splendor of the twelve Ādityas"—this refers to the Sun who possesses twelve digits; "homage to that splendor of his."

29b) By the Supreme Lord, the *kalā* [is formed]: a ā i ī u ū e ai o au aṃ aḥ. She whose nature is thus—homage be to her! And likewise, in the *Uttarabhāṣṭaka*: "By three, the three worlds... Thus, these three also have Tripurā as their essential nature, beginning with Brahmā.
She whose womb is filled with the state of Bhairava; she who is "Nānā," "Nanā," and "Namā"; I bow to her who is terrifying yet grants bliss, for she bestows the highest welfare.
In the void, situated within another void, she is called Haṃsā, the sustainer of the vital breath.
The vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is that which bears the name "Haṃsa"; "Ni-haṃsa" is exhalation, while "Haṃ" is inhalation.

That swan (*haṃsa*), with downward breath, sustains the life-force of the worlds through its form, existing in both gross and subtle states. The gross state is manifold and possesses many scriptures; the subtle is invisible and accessible only through knowledge. Between these two, established in the midst, is the mind, which takes up the *nama* and *yama*.
It is absorbed into itself;
(30a) whatever kind of knowledge has been perfected, it does not coexist with manifestation.
In both cases, one should always remain supported by mindfulness alone, like a person on a raft.
And likewise, from the beginningless and endless up to the end of the syllables,
there is the arrangement of Śiva, Śakti, and Haṃsa.
And having likewise induced the time of death and the deception of Mṛtyu,
they performed [the rite] in forward and reverse order, ending with the words situated in the middle.
Having understood this, the teaching [is given] at the end of the session.
One who has conquered the mind is always victorious over the objects of the senses;
however, when the mind remains unconquered, one is perpetually overcome by those very objects.
Therefore, the practitioner of the rite should make his own mind steady with effort;
when the mind is made steady, many accomplishments are achieved.
Austerity, Vedic study, and charity, even when undertaken at sacred fords or through sacrifices,
do not equal a sixteenth part of the awakening of the self through yoga.
There is nothing whatsoever superior to yoga as a medicine for the disease of saṃsāra;
knowing this, one should always practice yoga in such a manner.
30b) Likewise as before.
Victory to the Goddess, who is emptier than the empty, who dwells in the heart of the one whose vehicle is the swan,
the eternal Mistress who sustains the vital breath, the soul of the universe, the Mother!
In the one called Lambā, the supreme goddess flows toward the south and the north;

she is the *piṅgalā* who moves both south and north, the power (*śakti*) of Śiva. She flows neither to the south nor to the north, but flows between them. Established at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), that supreme goddess is Mahāmāyā, known as Lambā.
That very one called Laṃbā, in whose presence the three worlds are established, is seen at that moment as she who is named Sālambā;
however, she is to be contemplated by the eye of wisdom as the Supreme Goddess. And so it is said in the Uttara:
"Endowed with the rays of omniscience, devoid of existence and non-existence,
not bestowing pleasure due to dissolution, eternal, and situated upon the head of Śiva— she is Śivā."
"Supreme, moving from south to north. In Lākula, one should touch the seat on the path that is to be split by the two vowels (31a).
The divisions are ten, consisting of earth, cow, moon, and sky, joined with the crescent moon and the ether.
I have forgotten the mantra that reveals the time of death for these beings.
This is the seed-syllable of the southern and northern [paths]; therefore, one should always practice its recitation.
Thus it is stated in the Niśottara.

At the end of the night, she who desires to be seen, moving like the sun and moon, bestows form upon the world; she is the life-breath of the universe and the protector of its creation and destruction.
When it has emerged at the tip of the nose, the thread flows through the center.

When it has emerged at the tip of the nose, it is completely severed; like a thread stretched between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, it emerges and flows, flows and flows. This is the application of the union within the hollow of the skull. Therein, by means of the place...
It destroys merit. Suṣumnā and Sarasvatī are those two channels in the center; they are for the purpose of reciting the mantra in sequence.
She is Mahāmāyā. And so it is said in the Bhairavatantra: "Success is not described as being attained through that [mantra] when it is merely mental.
"The destroyer of obstacles and the bestower of liberation [is attained] through the sequential recitation of the mantra. Thus [it is said]. "In the center is the channel that carries the thread."
O Hṛllekhā, supreme bliss, you are established in the palate and at the crown of the head.

At the palate and the crown of the head is the Śaṅkhinī, located at the gateway four finger-breadths inside the root of the nose; its door is with the conch. It flows in the heart, the seat of the seed-syllable. She is supreme bliss, whose nature is supreme bliss, the Great Māyā; thus she is merged in the vision of the Uttara, free from existence and non-existence, and situated within the Kula.
She whose nature is gentle, who holds the moon, knowledge, and ignorance in her hands, O Lord of Gods; she who is saluted by the lords of the gods, who holds a lotus and a bud in her hands;

she who is fire, the divider, and the lineage of Kumāra; she who is Kāleśvara, the awakener, and the lake; she who is Nandā, the supreme, who has gone beyond both the higher and the lower; she who is Śakti, the ancient one, and the most exalted—thus she is praised.
In the throat of the nāda, which is adorned with the eight qualities (guṇāṣṭaka)—
the eight qualities being those external objects such as the eight supernatural powers (aṇimā etc.)— he speaks again of the eightfold quality.

Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—these are the eight qualities (*guṇa*). These eight qualities do not exist as modifications in the *puruṣa*, yet he is endowed with these eight qualities. By this, the qualities are established within the heart. Rubbed by the knot of *nāda*, they are established through being rubbed; [this occurs] by way of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

The skull-cup joined with the skull-cup at the door of the Śaṅkhinī; the Śaṅkhinī with the door, the throat with the heart, and the heart with the seat of the vital breath—thus he unites them in the ritual procedure.
"Rubbed against the knot of the throat from of old. This means that, by piercing the six locations, the sound has emerged; it moves both downward and upward.

Having first held the Lord of the Flame (Śikhīśa), one should cause the left [channel] to rise upward. The aperture of Dhanañjaya is to be pierced, adorned with the tone of the Sun. Joined with the Bindu and the Moon, it is seen as the seed-syllable of the Adamantine Throat (Vajra-kaṇṭhika).
The senses of life.
And likewise, in the Tripurārṇava:
Having emerged from the place, I do not utter the sixfold great mantra consisting of mantras and so forth which express the vowels, for the sake of determining the location.
"She is Mahāmāyā"—thus begins the praise by the Supreme Lord.
When the two-fold sheaths of merit and demerit, characterized by grossness and subtlety,
have been thoroughly agitated, that which is liberated from both existence and non-existence is called "gross-subtle."

She is the Supreme Self, existing in the form of all things mobile and immobile; you are free from passion—this is the meaning. Dharma and adharma refer to merit and demerit. Sukha and duḥkha refer to pleasure and pain.
The *saṃyogapuṭa* [method]; likewise at night.
Transcending the gross and the subtle, devoid of agitated states of being—
that establishment of sin and merit is manifested as Mahāmāyā.
In the state of the effect, cause, and agent, which is the triple void and the form of *nāda*,
the principles of *nādavigrahā* and *mṛtakuṇḍalī* constitute the realization of the way.
The state of the equal flavor of the three voids.

33a) It is empty of the moon, sun, and fire; it is immortal and without conflict from that state. It possesses all the planets, yet is free from the planets. Because it is the agency of both cause and effect, it is both the effect and the cause.
The state of being the agent of cause and effect is "causal agency" (*kāryakāraṇakartṛtva*). In that causal agency, [the self] exists in an unreal form. The cause is the reason;
just as a lamp within a jar is not seen due to its enclosure.
Likewise, that knowledge which follows its own course is also not within the range of vision; it is seen through the middle of the body by means of the veil of the sense-objects and faculties.
By means of the clarity of the guru’s instruction, cause the chapters to be released;
therefore, that which abides in the heart of the entire triple world is seen.
It is perceived as having the nature of cognition due to the relationship between cause and effect.
The supreme mantra that conquers death consists of the syllables *bhṛ-gā-bhi-tra-pa-re-phavā-sa-na*, with the vowel *ī* (long) applied, and is adorned at its peak by the three kinds of *bindus*.

The seed itself, which is cause and effect, is fully awakened in six months by the time of the *sukhadrā* [fruit]; for that which is born from death among living beings becomes recited, bold, and auspicious, even in the case of *Kāmākṣā*.
Neither empty nor non-empty, it pervades everywhere within the heart;
one should make emptiness itself manifest as the consort, issued forth from the supreme *māyā*.

In the supreme, non-supreme, and supremely pure consciousness—which is eternal, constant, and firm—the supreme-non-supreme [state] consists of the left and the right, [and] sin and merit; by these it is pervaded. In the supreme, the non-supreme, impure consciousness is accompanied by volition; it is eternal, constantly served, indestructible, and firm.

They attain certainty, immovability, and invisibility; because of its immortality, they obtain it. By means of that immortal practice, they sustain the life of the entire world. It destroys old age, death, and disease. Therefore, it is called eternal consciousness (*caitanya*). And so it was said by the ancients:
O Goddess, who pervades the high and the low within the Supreme, who brings joy to the world, who is consciousness and imperishable, and who is eternal— salutations be to you!
Thus was Mahāmāyā exhausted by that [labor].
The Goddess who bears all colors is established in the secret reality (*guhyatattva*). She who bears all colors consists of thirty-three letters, the white and other colors, and the fourth color.
All these are pervasive, having the form of space and the nature of wind, within the *samāna* wind, in the midst of the *apāna* wind.
She is established like a particle of frost; by this she is born. Therefore, the Goddess is called the bearer of all colors.

Abiding in the secret place, she is established in her secret form as the savior of the world, that Mahāmāyā. Thus, in the Vaināyaka Tantra: "From the letter *a* to the letter *ha*, she is established as the source of mantra; from the earth element to the end of the vowels (*i*), let the secret reality be revealed."

And likewise, in the *Kulakulārṇava*: "That goddess Kujā, whose name is ninefold, is the secret reality to be concealed; she is the one who pervades the world of men and speech, established as the secret Mahāmāhā."

The Goddess who sustains the world, existing in the world through conventional reality; she is the support of the worlds, the sustainer of the world. "World" refers to the three realms, including humans and the rest.
The Goddess Jagaddhāraṇī [is so called] because she sustains living beings from the bonds of saṃsāra, which consist of manifold sufferings.

*Saṃvṛti* is origination; its path is one that perceives like a road through *saṃvṛti*. At the time of origination, one should contemplate the lunar disk, and at the time of cessation, one should meditate on the solar disk. For that reason, it is not called "the path of worldly convention. Likewise, the nihilist [speaks of] dissolution, origination, and protection.
The protector of the family; her perfection extends to the end of the eon; she is the bestower of the giver of happiness.
35a) O bodiless Great Illusion, you who ferry one across the ocean of saṃsāra! The "ocean" refers to the great sea; saṃsāra itself is the sea.
To reach its further shore—that which is immeasurable and infinite—may come about through the grace of the Goddess. How is the Goddess bodiless? [For she exists] within the body.

She is devoid [of attributes]; she is Mahāmāyā. Śrīkaṇṭha, born from the Bindu, Krodhīśa, Śvapiñākī, Yugeśvara, and Ślaukha—these are said to be the seed-syllables of the body. She is the supreme thread of consciousness. And so it is stated in the *Uttaradarśanī*: "The supreme light, established in the mind, partless, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods."
O Mother, whose nature is the cause of creation, sustenance, and dissolution; O eternal and infinite embodiment of power, full of compassion—salutations to you!
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā; Jayā is the mind, Vijayā is wind, and Jayantī is the body; situated in the midst of those is Aparājitā. b)

She is Aparājitā because she conquers the senses that have been defeated. And so it was said previously: "The unconquered Mother, the other, the radiant bestower of perfection; Jayantī, Karuṇā, Cetā, Mahāmāyā, and Manonmanī."
Obeisance to you, the liberator from sin, who resides within the seed-syllable *tumburī*.
*Tumburī* is space (*ākāśa*). She stands in the midst of that; she who stands in the midst of space is the *tumburī*-seed.

The nature of the mantra is its own form. And Mahākāla is formed by the letter *pi*, the *inākī* (the letter *na*), the sword (*kha*), the *brahmagā* (the letter *ga*), the *vālīsāghīśaśī* (the letter *sa*), the *bindu* (the nasal dot), and *tumburī* (the letter *u*), which is not to be destroyed. Thus it is said in the Uttara: "At the end of the class [of consonants], joined with *ma*, *ra*, and the fourth [consonant], conjoined with the moon and the *bindu*, this is the seed-syllable of the power (*śakti*) known as Tumburī."
The Goddess, who effects bondage and liberation, is established at the end of the sixteen;
"bondage" refers to the bondage of saṃsāra. (36a)
By that, she is the bringer of liberation as well. Sin and merit: sin leads to the state of hell, while merit leads to the state of heaven.

She who bestows knowledge, which effects the severance of these two, is Mahāmāyā. Established at the end of the sixteen, she is the bond of the essence of thought; from her, liberation arises. Abiding at the end of the sixteen, she is the all-pervading void.
It enters the solar disc; for him, there is liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra. And likewise on the right.
O Goddess who binds with nooses, O giver of liberation, O Goddess who dwells within the peaceful heart of all beings, O Mistress of the Night,
salutations be unto you!
The Bhramani Shakti is endowed with a trident and a great array.

The *vyūha* is a collection; she is established as the assembly of all deities, situated in the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*. "Bhrāmanī," "bhramanī," "valambatitī," and "bhrāmanī" mean that she exists. How so? The Great Array (*mahāvyūha*) is the Protector of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*). She is the Yoginī whose activity is within the field of Bhairava.
36b) The family tree (kulavṛkṣa), accompanied by many deities; situated within the Yoginī; triangular in shape.
In the corner within the triangle is the seed-syllable cluster of the goddess Mahāmāyā.
