The physical body (piṇḍa) should be situated in the place of the void (mara); the mind (manas) should be situated in the place of the body;
the mind should be situated in the place of knowledge (jñāna), and likewise, both the body and knowledge in the place of the void.
Wisdom is not devoid of the aggregate, nor is the aggregate devoid of wisdom;
there is no distinction between the two, as they abide in a state of equal flavor.

In the outer corner, she is established in the Kramaṇa [mudrā]. She is established with the horse (Aśvārūḍhā). At Prayāga, there is the Udumbara tree; [the deity] Haṃsagahvara has the form of Śrīvatsa. [The element is] Vāyu. [The mudrā is] Vaigā; the weapon is the banner (dhvaja); [the goddess is] Brāhmī. [The seat is] Chappā; [the face is] Agnimukha; [the posture is] Risitāsana; [the place is] Kāmarūpa; [the goddess is] Karālī. [This is] in the eastern corner.
She is established in Vārāṇasī; she is the tree, the cave of the bull, the form of the white lotus, the one with upward-pointing hair, and the one whose weapon is the mace.
37a) Māheśvarī; Kuṇḍī, Kurṇa; Keśīnagara; Ulkāmukhī; Vaḍavā, Valinī, Lohajaṅgha; Śākarī; Ūrdhvakeśa—these are situated in the southeast corner. Kārāgiri.

Aśokavṛkṣa, Mayūragahyara, Dhvajākṛti, Mahānalī, Daṇḍadhārī, Komārī, Āmrātikkeśvara, Pūtanā, Hatāpunarmahākrodha, Pīnākṣī, Mahājaṅgha, and Agnika— these are stationed in the southern corner. Kaḍavavṛkṣa.
Garuda-gahvara, Kalaśākṛti, Saumyamukhī, Vajradhārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Pareśvatīra, Prahlākṣī, Vīrejā, Trijaṭā, Ambikā, and Analeti— these are situated in the south-western corner.
Jayantī, Nimbavṛkṣa, Mahiṣagahvara, and Cāmbarākṛti.
Jvālāmukhī, Khaḍgadhārī, Vārāhī, Māyāpurī,
Kampinī, Bhīmanāda, Elāpurī, Kharānana, Śaṅkhakarṇa, and Mahāpreta— these [are they].
Residing in the western corner are Caritrā, Karañjavṛkṣa, Gajagahvara, Matsyayugalākṛti, Kṛṣṇadaṇḍā, Śaktidharī, Indrāṇī, Rājagṛha, Cipiṭanāsāsī, Eruṇḍā, Mahākarṇī,
Ghaṇṭārava, Atimukhī, and Mahātuṇḍā; these are in the northwestern corner.

Saṃsthi, Ūrjayanī, the Aśvattha tree, Pretagahvara, Chātrākṛti, Māhāmāyā, Pāśadhārī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kṣicaralohatātra, Kāśmīra, Mahāmegha, Lākarṇa, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Kailāya— these are situated in the northeast corner. Koṭivarṣa.
Vaṭavṛkṣa, Siṃhagahvara, Śaṅkhākṛti, Hetuka, Triśūladhārī, Cāṇḍāpṛṣṭāpura, Vidyutmukhī, Pañceśvara, Puṇyavardhana, and Kumbhākṣa. (38a)

Karṇoṭī—these are situated in the northeast corner. By one who has personally seen the various [teachings] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and Dīpa, and who is joined with the mantra, they attain supreme victory through the peace of the Great Lord, knowing the ritual procedure and having performed the arrangement of the great mantra. By this, all are established in the secret reality; by this...

By reason of this, she is endowed with the Great Array (mahāvyūha). And so it is said in the *Uttara*: "In the region from Indra to Īśāna, Mahāmāyā is fully established; that Sovereign of the Great Array, who is the foundation of the secret reality, is victorious."
"Bhramanī, bhrāmanī, gaurī, māyāyantrapravāhinī;

māyāyantra, yoniyantre"—thus [it is said]. In the great sixteen-spoked wheel (*ṣoḍaśāra-mahācakra*), she is "bhramitā" (whirling) and "bhrāmitā" (causing to whirl), meaning she causes movement. Gaurī is set in motion by the Great Fall (*mahāpāta*) within the wheels of saṃsāra; this is her emergence.

The agent of withdrawal; it is seedless; it becomes established in the seed. It becomes born; it becomes a child; it becomes a youth; again it becomes another wind; it becomes an elder, wrinkled and grey-haired.
There is birth; there is old age; there is the suffering of decay and death. By these means, the wheel of saṃsāra has been set in motion.

Likewise, at the great night (mahāniśā), it is made to revolve by the power of the wheel of saṃsāra in the form of the force of wandering. O you who flow as the machine of illusion, you who are the Yoni-mudrā—homage be to you! Thus.
In the pure state that holds only to that [object], mindfulness is fully developed within the mind.

*Smṛtisambarddharī* means that which increases mindfulness; it is established in the place of the mind. *Cittatanmātradhāriṇī*: because it maintains the form of that [object] by means of the mind, it is called *cittatanmātradhāriṇī*. It is *cittatanmātradhāriṇī* because the external form of that [object] does not exist at the tip of the nose due to any other cause. As previously stated by the yogi.
The form of the Goddess, consisting of the cultivation of gnosis, is maintained.
39a) Another form of Maherī has the appearance of a flame rising from a tree.
The goddess Svacchandabhairavī, the Krodhonmattabhairavī.

Svacchanda Bhairavī, the Lord of Aghora—she who has one face and sixteen arms—that Goddess has been obtained by you. Her own heaven is her will; by this she is Svacchanda (the Free). Bhairavī is she who wanders, whose form is compassion, who delights upon the power of control. Speaking in the state of knowledge as *ai* and *ī*, she is the giver of liberation. She is Krodhī (Wrathful).
Unmattabhairava—these are the eighty-four principal ones pervaded by the reality (tattva) of Bhairava. She is Mahāmāyā.

In that very manner, during the night of Dakṣiṇastanī, Bhairava and Bhairavī themselves arose as the pervasive Svacchanda; they are the intoxicated ones of supreme bliss, for Śiva and Śakti are non-different.
O Rudra, you have proclaimed that [the power] resides in the form of the fifty phonemes.
He who has become formidable through the five-syllabled form.

39b) Sixteen vowels; thirty-four consonants. The vowel is Śiva. The moon has sixteen digits (kalās), and the thirty consonants are the powers (śaktis). Through this, the nature of the fifty-syllable mantra is realized. Moreover:

Pervaded by the fifty Bhairavas, Rudrabhairava and Kṣetrapāla are one in meaning. O you who illuminate devotion in that ocean of the Kula and Akula! You whose forms are wind, fire, earth, water, and ether;
you who are the refuge and the universal form of this entire world; O Bhavadeha, the garland of the universe, bestower of supernatural powers and liberation!
"Victorious is the one Śakti, Kujā, whose nature is compassion. Thus, that Mahāmāyā, whose essential form consists of the fifty phonemes, was proclaimed by Rudra as Valī.
Salutation to Amṛtā, Ruru, Caṇḍā, Kāpālinī, and Śivā.

At the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*), Śiva becomes embodied as Kāpālinī, the bearer of the skull of Śiva. The state of being a *kāpālī* consists of the union of Śiva and Śakti, which is dark blue in color.
Here, "Ka" refers to Śiva, and "Pāla" refers to Śakti.
Who is Śiva? He who protects the body (kāya). Who protects the body? Kapālinī. In the one called Amṛta is Umāmaheśvara; his form is Ruru. Ruru is an asura; his enemy is Caṇḍa; thus, Rurucanda.

The meaning is that the goddesses known as Raktagaurī and Cakrikā have been pervaded by you. One should meditate on the lunar disc at the beginning of the teaching of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), [and] the seed-syllable of nectar as the great mantra in the middle of the palm. Thus it is said in the Uttara:
At the time of dissolution, she takes the form of Kālikā; she is the source of the gods beginning with Brahmā. Victorious is the goddess Caṇḍakāpālinī, the blood of creation!
O Rurukaṇī, O Mahāmāyā, salutations to you, Jñānabhairavī!
You are Rurukuṇī because you cause the destruction of the senses (indriya).
That by which the senses are destroyed is Mahāmāyā; salutations to her. All living beings are of the nature of gnosis (jñāna-rūpa), expanded through the activity of the Rajas aspect of Śakti’s Kalās.
By Śātyuka, [he knows] the divine, the royal, the human, the dark, and the animal; Bhairavī is as before, and likewise as previously stated.
Once born, the sense-faculties have arisen; at death, the flickering body is cast off.
Through the power of great illusion, there is the revolving of saṃsāra.

"O you with formidable fangs! O you with lightning-tongue! O you with eyes like stars! O you with a terrifying face!"—thus the hymn of praise addressed to the Supreme Lord includes these vocatives: "O you with formidable fangs (*daṃṣṭrotkaṭe*). Her fang is exceedingly radiant, possessing a luster like that of the moon. Her tongue is a "lightning-tongue," meaning a tongue that bites like lightning. "Eyes like stars": her eyes are like the *tārakā* constellations. Of this...

Like a flame; she whose eyes are [like that], O star-eyed one, O fearful-faced one (*bhayānanā*). "Fear" refers to the fear of *saṃsāra*; "O fearful-faced one" means [she who has] a face [as terrifying as] the sacrificial fire (*makha*). Likewise, in the case of Vaināyaka.
I bow to the form of Tāriṇī, who has fangs like the moon, whose lolling tongue is lightning, whose face is terrifying, and who destroys the fear of saṃsāra.

41a) I bow to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, O Aghorā of terrible form. "I bow" means I offer salutation. O Goddess of the lords of gods: the "lords of gods" refers to the thirty-three crores of deities; she is the goddess of those gods.

Trideva; the Lord of Trideva; Maheśvara—the meaning is the Protector (Nātha) of Maheśvara. That Goddess is the Sovereign of the Gods of Gods. In what form? In the form that is both non-terrible (Aghora) and terrible (Ghora). Aghora is the gentle form; Ghora is the fierce form. The power of Aghora effects the creation of the world; [the power of] Ghora is Śiva.
She causes the destruction of the world; she destroys for you the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. She is of non-terrible form.
Likewise, it is said in the Tripurārṇava:
I bow to the Mistress of the World, who dwells upon the head of Śiva,
who possesses a gentle form like that of the gods, who is beautiful, and whose nature is eternal.
Homage to you, Jvālāmukhī, the swift Umādevī!
Jvālāmukhī means "Fire-faced.

Vegavatī has the wind as her mouth; that is to say, fire is the wind. To you, O Goddess Umā, who pervades all through your dual nature, salutations! Likewise, the Ṛṣis Śata and Drtaśikhā likewise move upon the eastern seat.

One should pierce the supreme sound with the side-limb; the protection of the three seed-syllables consists of Jvālāmukha and the others. Likewise, in the Bhairava-tantra, Jvālāmukha and the face of Vāyu are of one essence and all-pervading.
O Goddess Umā, whose nature is sound, the Great Māyā—salutations to you!

Yogeśī, Śrīdevī, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; Yogeśī is the sixty-fourth Yoginī, and among them, Mahāmāyā is preeminent in Yoga. Śrīdevī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are the Goddess of the Three Junctions (Trisandhyā); thus Śrīdevī is Gāyatrī. She has four arms and holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

She holds a rosary and the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing wealth. She has a swan as her vehicle, is red in color, appears like a sixteen-year-old maiden, and has loose, disheveled hair.
At the break of dawn, they contemplate Lakṣmī and Sāvitrī, who are four-armed.

Sarasvatī is renowned as having four arms; she holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a jewel. She is seated upon Garuḍa, is dark-complexioned, and youthful. She is to be meditated upon at midday. [Another form] holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), a rosary (akṣasūtra), a book, and displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya); she has a swan as her vehicle and is seated upon a lotus. She is yellow-complexioned and aged; she is to be meditated upon in the afternoon.

The upper half [of her body] is black at midnight; below that, the thighs are white; and below those, the feet are yellow. She has three faces, and their colors are likewise [as described]. She rides a lion, has six arms, and holds a wheel of eyes, a sword, and a trident, while displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. Adorned with all ornaments, she rests upon a lotus and a skin during the midnight hour.

One should contemplate thus regarding the eyes: "O you who possess the form of the twilight’s turning away, pure as the moon, you alone are the essence of color and form; in this world of saṃsāra, you are the one who severs the bondage of the noose and destroys dullness here. (42b)

I bow to the primordial Liṅga, which is the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśanātha), who bestows supreme bliss upon yogins, whose splendor is meditated upon by them, whose body is nectar, and who is saluted by the best of gods.
One should meditate upon Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Bhṛgu, Ananta, Sarasvatī, and Māyā, who are as radiant as the moon, while performing the *sandhyā* rite.
Among these meditations on time, the flickering nature of death is supreme; it is neither with nor against the hair.

The goddess Haṃsavāgīśvarī, Gomukhī, Śaktimālinī, Haṃsavāgīśvarī Svarī, Sarasvatī, Haṃsavāhanasarasvatī, Gomukhī Parameśvarī, and Kubjikā—these are the nine types. They are: Bāla (1), Madhya (2), and Jyeṣṭhā (3). Each of these has three further divisions.
Śrī Kubjikā is Mahāmāyā. She is called Mālinī because she destroys impurity (*mala*); thus, she is the Destroyer of Impurity (*malanāśanī*). What is that impurity?
It is the impurity born of *āṇava*, *māyā*, and *karman*. That which is produced by *māyā* is "born of *māyā*" (*māyaja*). (43a)

Furthermore: the impurity of delusion (*moha-mala*), attachment, aversion, anger, greed, smell, taste, touch, form, and sound—these are the ten impurities by which a person is soiled; thus she is *Mālinī*. Moreover, in another way, *Mālinī* falls as an unbroken stream from the stainless [source] to the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*). She is the *Mālinī* of the common support (*sādhāra-mālinī*). Furthermore:
When darkness prevails at the dissolution of the three worlds,

Then, filled with splendor, that Mālinī shone throughout the three worlds. At that time, having seen the radiance of her own form, Kujā—the Śrī who was deluded by pride—offered praise to Prabhāmālinī. She is Mālinī; she is pervaded by the Goddess Mahāmāyā, as well as by the Great Imperishable (Mahākṣara).
Having reversed the vowels and separated them with the anusvāra, [one obtains] Haṃsa-vāgīśvarī-jayā. A wise person should recite this at dawn during the morning twilight as the conqueror of death.
And likewise in the *Uttara* [Tantra].
For Mālinī is the nature of power, as are Mahāmāyā and Kālikā;
she is eternal, stainless, and free from blemish, the supreme refuge who bestows liberation.

Kroṣṭāṅgī, Subhagā, Devī, Durgā, and likewise Kātyāyanī—Kroṣṭāṅgī is the triangle in front; it is said that the eight [forms] of the Goddess are pervaded [by these]. Subhagā means "possessing beauty."
Durgā is of subtle form, and O Bhavati, your specific forms are established as Kātyāyanī; therefore, that goddess Kātyāyanī is one whose flower is the *sāmāsa*. Thus it was previously stated.
O Goddess Kāmākṣā, the bestower of boons, who resides in the city of the triangle;
O beautiful one, the savior of the world, O Kātyāyanī, salutations to you!

*Nityaṃ klinda* is declared to be *sā*; *rakta caikākṣarā* is the supreme *parā*. *Nityaṃ klindam* is established as *asti*; *sā* is so declared. *Rakta caikākṣara* consists of two syllables, *rakta*, which is the flower and fruit of Śiva and Śakti; [the first] is the red *repha*.
44a) Māṃsapuṣpa; the letter *kṣa* is semen (*śukra*), by way of its essence, the seed-syllable (*bīja*). The supreme [syllable] consists of a single letter.
Furthermore, she who possesses eight limbs within the triangular city is the destroyer of the eastern seat (*pīṭha*); she is Pannagā.
The red syllable *kṣoḥ* is this single-syllabled axe, possessing the supreme moon and the bindu.
It is single-syllabled by means of the letter *a*, all-pervading as the fifty [letters], and thus it rejoices.
The eternal mother of the world, red in color and enchanting, the single-syllabled Great Illusion who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation— she is Kujā.
You are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī;
you are Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā, O goddess with the terrifying face.
These are established as the mistresses of yoga.
O Goddess of gods, you are indeed the Mistress of Yoga, accompanied by the eight cruel goddesses.

For you are indeed the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśī). These eight Yoginīs are pervaded by you, O Mahāmāyā, together with the eight [deities] beginning with Iṣṭaka. [There are] the eight Kulas, the eight Vaṭukas, and so forth; Ka, Kaṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla.
Gaṇabhairava; Bhūta; Sasthiteśa in the cremation ground; Kṣetreśa—thus [they are] each accompanied by one Yoginī and joined with the eight beginning with Vaṭuka.
The Aindrī, Āgneyā, Yāmyā, Nairṛtyā,
Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, Kauverī, and Īśānī oceans were likewise seized.
Situated in order in the directions: south-east, south, south-west, west, north-west, north, and north-east;
and constantly meditating on the mantra beginning with "asāntam" before him, together with a wise counselor.
In the body, one encounters death, which moves in a sequential progression.
Priyā, Gaurī, Varuṇā, Kolā, Aṭṭahāsā, Jayantikā,
Caritrikā, and Varā— may these eight goddesses protect [me] in eight ways.

45a) These are established in the body at eight locations: Priyāgu is in the center of the seed (bīja); Kolāgiri is between Varuṇa and Agni; Aṭṭahāsa is in the blood; Jayantikā is in the flesh; and Caritrā is in the skin.

In the hair-pores is Ekāmbarā; the goddess Koṭa is at all the joints of the limbs; Brahmāṇī is in the secret place; Māheśvarī is in the heart; Komārī is in the face; Vaiṣṇavī is in the ear; Vārāhī is in the throat; Indrāṇī is at the junction of the mouth;
Caṇḍī is at the root of the nose; and Cāmuṇḍā is at the end of the twelve [fingers].

Likewise, during this great night, when the seed-syllables and so forth, the secret places and so forth, and Brahmā and the others are meditated upon as residing in their respective locations within the body, the perfection of yoga and a new lifespan shall be attained.
Immediately following that, the group of eight female messengers (dūtī) is described.
Likewise, O Kālī, O Umādūtī, O Devadūtī, salutations be unto you!
O Bhadrakālī, O Mahādevī, O Carmamuṇḍā, O terrifying one!
O Greatly Pure One, O Greatly Peaceful One, salutations to you who have the form of Śakti!
(45b) Established in this body in the form of these Śaktis: Kālī is in the head; the goddess Umā is on the crown; [and] in the left hand...

Devadūtī is in the right hand; Bhadrakālī is in the heart; Mahādevī is in the middle of the anus; Caṇḍamuṇḍā is in the left foot; Mahocchuṣmā is in the right foot; and Mahāśāntā is in the place of the single body. One should meditate upon the circle of Yoginīs, the Kṣatras, and the Dūtīs within one's own body.
In this way, when meditated upon within the body of the sequence, it is the deception of death;
likewise in the Daśakālī.
"The Dūtīcakra and the Kṣatra of the Yoginīs reside within the body;
one who knows them as situated in the body will certainly attain liberation. Thus [it is said].

"Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ" are the Mahāvyāhṛtis used in the fire-oblation (agnihoma). Bhūḥ is the world of the nāgas; Bhuvaḥ is the world of mortals; Svaḥ is the heavenly world. By means of this offering of oblations, one should cause [the soul] to ascend upward at the end of the word "Svaḥ."
One whose desire for food has ceased should avoid [eating] when it is in its own form or in another form;
by that, one is released from the Great Utterance (mahāvyāhṛti).

*Bhūḥ* is the left corner; *bhuvaḥ* is the right corner; *svaḥ* is in the middle corner. At the end of *svāhā*, [recite] "O all-pervading one, out of compassion, act for my sake! O Kurukālī and the others! Make the three worlds of equal flavor, and indeed make them of one essence! The lunar orb is the mortal world (*martyaloka*); the solar orb is the heavenly world (*svargaloka*); the fire orb is...

The netherworld (pātālaloka). The three mandalas and the three worlds must not be differentiated. That [mantra] is divided into two parts by the supreme *hārepha* (the letter *ha*), increased by the *pīṭha* (the letter *i*) and the sun (*divākara*, the letter *ra*), and adorned with the crescent moon (*khaṇḍa*) and the lunar dot (*bindu*). This mantra pervades the three worlds; when meditated upon, it bestows the accomplishment of all aims.

The excellent night and day throughout the three times are clearly destroyed by death. Through a state of differentiation, there is no liberation; through a state of non-differentiation—in the movement of the syllable-less reality—one becomes a possessor of accomplishment.
Free from duality, devoid of mental practice, without qualities yet the knower of qualities—
this is declared to be the state of Brahman, the independent and imperishable state.
Without appearance, without bliss, without form, and without agitation;
here, everything transcends form, being neither non-existence nor a knower.
When the proponent's position and the opponent's position have been exhausted, one's own position is devoid of positions;
for the destruction of the bondage of birth, it destroys the triad of positions.
On a path devoid of the three wombs, silent and free from sound;
when the state of uniformity is attained, there is neither bliss nor meditative cultivation.
Three, one, three, and one— devoid of *jñāna*,
devoid of *haṃsa*, it is declared to be the imperishable (*avyaya*) that effects the severing of the bonds (*pāśa*).
One should meditate on everything as empty through this very conventional usage.

O Mantra! Having been awakened by the three realms, the two truths, the three times, and the three [jewels], one should contemplate *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ* as eternally to be realized day and night.
In the body, in external knowledge, and in the homa-mind and the oblations—
as it is likewise stated in the *Uttara*.
The wise man who meditates upon the four junctions of the day, beginning with the Gāyatrī,
shall be liberated from all sins and become a partaker of liberation.
O Mahāmāyā, you who seek knowledge, I desire to know this:

for a person seeking knowledge, O Mahāmāyā, liberation from the ocean of saṃsāra occurs through knowing and understanding by means of knowledge; thus, the conceptualization of saṃsāra is a dualistic method.
Or the ocean, or a tree.
The sense-faculties are like lotuses born in the water of suffering and pleasure;
this birth is the near shore, while the next birth is the further shore beyond.
And by means of the mouth of the Guru, one shall reach the further shore;
it originates from the seed of the Unmanifest and is endowed with the root of the intellect.
Egoity is its great trunk, the five [elements] are its roots and its sprouts;
the objects and the senses are the tips of its leaves, and it is endowed with the mind as its flower.
Having mounted the thread of knowledge, one should consume the two fruits of pleasure and pain, which are joined with the bark-garment of existence, in order to attain the desired liberation.
They too [attained] the supreme state.
Therefore, one who has mastered the senses through constant and correct practice of knowledge [attains] that which illuminates correct knowledge through the supreme practice of the senses.
O humans, whoever recites this stream [of mantras] at the three junctions of the day,
and whoever recites this Great Māyā-mantra at the time of the three junctions— this very mantra which is being recited.
One obtains the desired objects of thought; one becomes the most excellent among women.

Whatever task is intended by those women, they obtain the desired objects of thought. This is called "the fulfillment of desires. One becomes beloved by women; one becomes beloved by young maidens. By whichever man this Mahāmāyā is recited, [he attains these results].
Through that nectar of immortality, one attains the desired world; one lives happily in the Blessed One, by which person they understand the fourfold path.
48a) The four deities: likewise on the new moon day; the single-faced one, the single-existence, the three-formed, the complete, the full-moon mistress in the east;
the mistress of beings, she who resembles the sky, the Blessed One, the eternal mistress in the south; [she] who is accessible through knowledge.
I bow to Kujesvarī, who dwells in the Kula, the singer in the western direction,
the illustrious Vāmā, the Mother of the Universe, Darśeśvarī, and Kālikā;

she who is differentiated by name in the center of the ritual procedure, mounted upon the syllables of the Nāga, the Moon, the beautiful Bindu, the Vedas, and the Svara, and established upon Bhṛgu and Śiva.
I bow to her who goes to the end of the path, who for the Sun [is] the Moon struck by the note *Sva*, and who is the eternal support through *māyā* at the end of the sacrifice;

she who destroys the body of suffering and cuts away the fear of *saṃsāra*. She whose name consists of four syllables is the mantra of the state of the four aims of life. This is declared to be the Bhairava mantra: O Mahāmāyā, salutations to you!
Thus ends the Mokṣasopāna-ṭīkā.
